criteria.quote: Graveler climbs mountains just to roll back down.
criteria.revision: Replace the generic “just” framing with a more evidence-specific reversal: “Graveler climbs from a mountain’s base to the summit, crunching rocks all the way—then rolls back to the bottom.”

criteria.quote: At the mountain's base, Graveler starts climbing while crunching rocks.
criteria.revision: Add the concrete food detail: “Graveler climbs toward the summit while crunching mossy rocks—its favorite food.”

criteria.quote: Why does Graveler climb all the way up?
criteria.revision: The research does not explain why Graveler climbs, so make the open loop answerable: “What happens when Graveler finally reaches the summit?”

criteria.quote: At the mountain's base, Graveler starts climbing while crunching rocks.
criteria.revision: Replace the repeated eating beat with a scale increase: “It can eat a ton of rocks a day, then keeps climbing toward the summit.” Follow that with the supported speed escalation: “Once it rolls back down, its speed can exceed 60 mph.”

criteria.quote: The summit is not the destination. It is the starting line for Graveler's descent.
criteria.revision: The reversal is revealed in the title and first scene, so delay it. Change the title to “Graveler Eats Its Way Up a Mountain,” let the opening cover only the climb and feast, and reveal at the summit: “As soon as it reaches the peak, it rolls back down the way it came.”

criteria.quote: At the mountain's base, Graveler starts climbing while crunching rocks.
criteria.revision: The rock-eating idea is repeated in the next scene. Give each beat a distinct fact: base-to-summit climbing, mossy rocks and a ton per day, the immediate summit turn, then momentum exceeding 60 mph and obstacles being rolled over.

criteria.quote: The summit is not the destination. It is the starting line for Graveler's descent.
criteria.revision: Replace the metaphorical restatement with the stronger documented outcome: “Upon reaching the peak, Graveler rolls back down to the bottom—and with enough momentum, its speed can exceed 60 mph.”

criteria.quote: Is this brilliant efficiency, or the strangest commute?
criteria.revision: “Efficiency” and “commute” are interpretations the research does not establish. Ask a factual split instead: “Is Graveler’s mountain trip mainly a feeding route—or a rolling route with a meal on the way?”
